about: Questions and answers: for every guest answer of 30 or more words, gpt-6.1-sol (medium effort) wrote interview-style questions about how the guest understands an entity or event. Only questions whose answer shows judgment or taste were kept, each asks one thing and stands alone, and each answer is the guest's own reply, synthesized from the transcript (rewritten in the first person, filler removed, fragments joined). Every supporting quote was checked word for word against the transcript.
Categories are assigned per guest by hand from each question and answer; each question has exactly one.

Rubrics: the same v10 rubric writer as the raw-transcript evaluation (here run with gpt-6.1-sol at medium effort) turned each guest answer into one-idea criteria. One answer produced no rubrics and is unscored.

Answers: each model saw a one-line host introduction naming the guest, then the question, and answered as the guest at xhigh effort with no browsing or tools. Claude models ran through claude -p; GPT models through codex exec.
Judge: gpt-6-luna at high effort with the same core-criterion prompt as the raw-transcript evaluation (which used gpt-5.6-luna). The guest's answer is withheld from the judge.

Caveats: Claude answers ran much longer than GPT answers (median 217 to 439 words versus 72 to 161), and longer answers have more chances to cover a rubric. Haiku 5.5 declined 6 of the 181 questions (4 Karthik, 2 Ilya, none for Ray Dalio), saying it would not invent first-person speech for a real person; declines count as misses. Ilya Sutskever's views are widely discussed and this November 2025 episode may be in some models' training data, so his scores can reflect recall of the interview as well as shared thinking.

Ray Dalio (The Diary Of A CEO, July 2026): questions, rubrics, answers and judging follow exactly the same steps and models, from his ElevenLabs transcript. His views on debt cycles and the "big cycle" are laid out at length in his books, so models can draw on published material as well as shared thinking.
Scores measure coverage of the ideas in the guest's actual answer, not overall answer quality. ASR and speaker labels may contain errors.

items.question: What purpose do you find most interesting for an AI benchmark?

items.question: How do you understand the apparent performance gap between convolutional networks and vision transformers through your work on “A ConvNet for the 2020s”?
items.object: The performance gap between convolutional networks and vision transformers
items.reference: So that was a really interesting story. We were working on this paper in 2021, and back then, transformers had just entered the computer vision research space through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community had been switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they were getting better and better performance. So in this work, we wanted to investigate whether truly convnets had lost their competitiveness, and whether it's possible to control all the design components to study whether convnets can be modernized to be on par with vision transformers at that time. We wanted to study whether the seeming performance gap between vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution, or due to other seemingly small design details. And we found the answer to be the latter. So after a lot of studying, of modernizing the design components of a convnet, we eventually got the model to be on par with very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that no matter whether you choose convnets or vision transformers, as long as you get everything correct, you'll get the same frontier-level performance on vision tasks.

items.question: How do you assess the importance of neural network architecture choice for making AI more useful?
items.object: Neural network architecture choice and its practical importance
items.reference:

I would say, as long as you get everything correct, as long as you explore the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. I think in the past many years, there haven't been innovations that have been widely adopted other than the mature architectures that we already were working with several years ago.

items.question: How do you assess whether internet-scale computer vision datasets are broad enough to support models that generalize to every task?
items.object: The breadth of internet-scale computer vision datasets
items.reference:
So I will first talk a little bit about the context. This paper is more vision-focused. Over years, people have been developing larger and larger datasets, from more and more diverse sources. Initially we had MNIST, and then CIFAR, and then ImageNet, and then internet-scale datasets like DataCamp or Conceptual Captions, CC, from Google. They have seemingly more and more diverse images, and they are larger and larger, from tens of thousands to billion scale. It was kind of tempting to make the assumption that we are already good with datasets because it's really all the things you can get from the internet. But in some of our initial experiments, we found that these datasets are still nothing like each other.

We designed a very dumb experiment that doesn't make sense at all as a deep learning training program. Given three very large-scale computer vision datasets, we train a neural network to classify which dataset a particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem; it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. It's a multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, higher than 80% when you have three datasets. The random guessing accuracy would be 33%, but the model can be much better than that. So this means, to a model, these datasets are still very, very different. It has very clear cues to tell which dataset this image comes from. Of course, we are doing this on held-out validation sets. We are not predicting the training images.

But still, this has been surprisingly accurate, and that prompts us to reflect: have we really been successful in curating a large-scale, all-encompassing dataset, at least in the computer vision domain? What kind of dataset is the end goal? It's kind of hard to define this so-called all-encompassing global distribution dataset. Different people might have different criteria, and it might not be a reasonable assumption there.

A big story of the success of LM is that it's not a domain-specific model, right? We want the model to be able to do everything, and a common assumption is that we need the model to have seen everything during training. How much progress are we making on that? It seems from this initial experiment that we haven't reached that point yet, and it still makes sense to think about how we curate these datasets for the model to be really generalizing to every task we want the model to be good at.

items.question: How do you make sense of the gap between AI models’ strong evaluation results and their much weaker real-world performance and economic impact?
items.object: The disconnect between AI models’ evaluation performance and real-world performance
items.reference: This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. You look at the evals and you go, "Those are pretty hard evals." They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of how the model can, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation. An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, "Can you please fix the bug?" And the model says, "Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that." And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, "You have this new second bug," and it tells you, "Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again," and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, "Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing." From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, "Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?" I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

items.question: How do you think about the usefulness of a value function in reinforcement learning?
items.object: Value functions in reinforcement learning
items.reference: When people do reinforcement learning, the way reinforcement learning is done right now, how do people train those agents? You have your neural net and you give it a problem, and then you tell the model, "Go solve it." The model takes maybe thousands, hundreds of thousands of actions or thoughts or something, and then it produces a solution. The solution is graded. And then the score is used to provide a training signal for every single action in your trajectory. That means that if you are doing something that goes for a long time—if you're training a task that takes a long time to solve—it will do no learning at all until you come up with the proposed solution. That's how reinforcement learning is done naively. That's how o1, R1 ostensibly are done. The value function says something like, "Maybe I could sometimes, not always, tell you if you are doing well or badly." The notion of a value function is more useful in some domains than others. For example, when you play chess and you lose a piece, I messed up. You don't need to play the whole game to know that what I just did was bad, and therefore whatever preceded it was also bad. The value function lets you short-circuit the wait until the very end. Let's suppose that you are doing some kind of a math thing or a programming thing, and you're trying to explore a particular solution or direction. After, let's say, a thousand steps of thinking, you concluded that this direction is unpromising. As soon as you conclude this, you could already get a reward signal a thousand timesteps previously, when you decided to pursue down this path. You say, "Next time I shouldn't pursue this path in a similar situation," long before you actually came up with the proposed solution.
